text:
The minister, pictured above speaking at the South African Nuclear and Clean Energy Conference last week, said state-owned Eskom had submitted its feasibility report for the extra capacity, which is scheduled to be on stream by 2039 under 2025’s Integrated Resource Plan.
He said the department was "preparing a proposed determination for public participation … publication of the determination is a statutory trigger for procurement". The aim is for the final determination by the end of April 2027 "and then we will start the process of building 5.2 GW of nuclear", he said.
In his speech he said that small modular reactors would have a place in the country: "For South Africa, the first question is which industrial users have a heat or power requirement that can support a project of that scale. Smaller units can spread capital commitments over time. The expected savings from factory production depend on repeat orders and a supply chain that can deliver them. We will assess the economics of the first units separately from those assumed for a mature production line and establish the licensing and fuel requirements for the designs under consideration.
"The Department is taking forward the socio-economic impact and cost-benefit study that will inform the Nuclear Industrialisation Plan. I expect that work to identify the procurement packages that can sustain South African production, the firms already able to compete and the capabilities we must develop before tenders are issued."
There also a need to cultivate a pipeline for skills in the country, he said: "One of the biggest inherent risks in this programme is that we have not built a nuclear power plant in the past 50 years or so … at Koeberg, they know how to run an already-built power station. So, the inherent risk is we don't have people who have built nuclear power stations before."
South African Nuclear Energy Corporation (Necsa) said it welcomed the confirmation of a ministerial determination for the procurement of the 5.2 GW of new capacity, as well as decisions which will see it "advancing efforts to re-establish South Africa's front-end nuclear fuel cycle capabilities, particularly uranium conversion, enrichment and fuel fabrication. These initiatives will reduce reliance on imported fuel and secure supply for existing and future reactors and embed local industry in the nuclear value chain, creating skilled jobs and a more resilient supply chain for the country's new-build programme".
Necsa said the decision, a year ago, to move the Pebble Bed Modular Reactor (PBMR) programme out of care and maintenance provided "an opportunity to assess the intellectual property retained from the programme and explore its potential applications and future utilisation. This preserves a base of reactor engineering expertise and coated-particle fuel research. Necsa will use it to assess industrial opportunities, including small modular reactor applications, and to develop high-temperature gas-cooled reactor fuel, scaling up from the Fuel Development Laboratory towards a pilot plant".
The PBMR was to have been a small-scale high-temperature reactor using graphite-coated spherical uranium oxycarbide tristructural isotropic (TRISO) fuel, with helium as the coolant, able to supply process heat as well as generating electricity. Based on well-proven German technology, South Africa had been working on the PBMR project since 1993, and PBMR Ltd was established in 1999 with the intention of developing and marketing the reactor. However, in 2010 the then government formally announced its decision no longer to invest in the project, which was then placed under care and maintenance.
Earlier this year Necsa launched an Expression of Interest process which aimed "to identify capable technology partners … to advance a fit-for-purpose SMR technology for future deployment".
South Africa currently has two nuclear power reactors at Koeberg with a capacity of 1.85 GW, generating about 5% of the country's electricity. The units entered commercial service in 1984 and 1985 respectively.
